procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 8, 1969 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Application No. 1341 of 1968 refusing to quash the order of committal passed by the Magistrate.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed an application in the High Court under sec. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the committal order. The appellant argued that no consent, as required by s. 196A(1) Cr.P.C., having been obtained, the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence of conspiracy. The High Court dismissed the application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate's jurisdiction to take cognizance of a case is vitiated by the lack of prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, when the offence of criminal conspiracy was not alleged in the initial police report but was considered by the Magistrate at the later committal stage.

facts: The police filed a charge-sheet against the appellant for offences including abetment of forgery and impersonation (ss. 419/109, 468, 471 IPC).
The charge-sheet did not allege the offence of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
The Magistrate took cognizance of the case based on this police report.

At a later stage, during committal proceedings, the Magistrate framed charges against the appellant that included criminal conspiracy (s. 120B), the object of which was to commit a non-cognizable offence (forging a passport).
No prior consent for initiating proceedings for criminal conspiracy was obtained as required by Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
law: Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code prohibits a court from taking cognizance of the offence of criminal conspiracy (s. 120B IPC) where its object is to commit a non-cognizable offence, unless prior consent from the government has been obtained.
Under Section 190 of the Cr.P.C., a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence when they first take judicial notice of it, typically upon receiving a police report or a complaint.
The relevant test is to determine what offence was "primarily and essentially" disclosed by the allegations in the documents upon which cognizance was taken, not just the sections of law mentioned.
application: The Supreme Court drew a crucial distinction between the initial act of "taking cognizance" and the subsequent act of "framing charges."

The Court determined that the Magistrate takes cognizance of the offences alleged in the police report at the time it is filed. In this case, the police report alleged abetment of forgery and impersonation, not criminal conspiracy.
The materials before the Magistrate at the cognizance stage, including the charge-sheet and witness statements, prima facie disclosed the offence of abetment.

The fact that the Magistrate, at the later committal stage, decided that the same facts warranted a more appropriate charge of criminal conspiracy did not change the nature of the offence for which he had initially taken cognizance.

Since the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence of abetment (for which no consent is needed), and not criminal conspiracy, the condition precedent of obtaining consent under Section 196A(2) was not applicable at that initial, critical stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the Magistrate's jurisdiction was not vitiated. The Court reasoned that the Magistrate took cognizance of the offences alleged in the police report, which did not include criminal conspiracy. Therefore, the requirement for prior consent under Section 196A(2) was not triggered at the cognizance stage, and the subsequent framing of a conspiracy charge did not retroactively invalidate the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the specific sections mentioned in the police report or on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations.

facts: The police filed a charge-sheet against the appellant, alleging offences of abetment of forgery and false impersonation under various sections of the Penal Code.
The charge-sheet did not mention the offence of criminal conspiracy (s. 120B).
The Magistrate took cognizance of the case based on this police report.
At a later stage, when framing charges, the Magistrate concluded that the materials warranted a charge of criminal conspiracy (s. 120B) rather than just abetment.
The appellant argued that the Magistrate could not take cognizance of the case because the facts disclosed a criminal conspiracy, which required a prior sanction under s. 196A(2) of the Cr.P.C.
law: The court affirmed the principle established in prior cases that when determining which offence to take cognizance of, it is not the specific sections mentioned in a complaint or police report that matter, but the offence that is prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations.
The proper test is to examine the allegations to determine the offence that is "primarily and essentially" disclosed.
application: The Court distinguished between the initial stage of taking cognizance and the later stage of framing charges.
It reasoned that when the Magistrate first took judicial notice of the case, he did so based on the offences alleged in the police report.
The offence "primarily and essentially" disclosed in that report was abetment of forgery and false impersonation, not criminal conspiracy.
Therefore, the cognizance taken by the Magistrate was for the offences of abetment and forgery.
The Magistrate's subsequent decision to frame a charge for criminal conspiracy did not retroactively change the nature of the offence for which he had initially taken cognizance.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations in the police report, not just the specific sections mentioned. In this case, the Magistrate took cognizance of the offences of abetment and forgery as alleged in the report, and therefore, the sanction required for a conspiracy charge was not a condition precedent for taking cognizance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate's jurisdiction to take cognizance of a case is vitiated by the lack of prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, when the offence of criminal conspiracy was not alleged in the initial police report but was considered by the Magistrate at the later committal stage.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the committal order should be quashed because it included a charge for criminal conspiracy (Section 120B), which requires prior consent under Section 196A(2) for the initiation of proceedings.
The appellant contended that since the Magistrate ultimately framed a charge of criminal conspiracy, the entire proceeding was invalid from the start due to the absence of the required consent.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as reflected in the court's reasoning, was that the requirement for consent must be assessed at the time the Magistrate takes cognizance of the case.
At the stage of taking cognizance, the police charge-sheet did not allege or charge the accused with criminal conspiracy.

The Magistrate's decision to frame a charge of criminal conspiracy at the later committal stage does not retroactively invalidate the initial, lawful act of taking cognizance based on the original charge-sheet.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of an offence for the purpose of taking cognizance depends on the specific sections mentioned in the police report or on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations.
appellant_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the appellant's argument on this specific legal principle. Their main argument focused on the consequence of the final charge framed by the magistrate, implying that the substance of the case (which they believed was conspiracy) should have governed the need for sanction from the outset.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, which the court accepted, is that the necessity of sanction depends not on the specific sections mentioned in a complaint or police report, but on the offence that is prima facie disclosed by the facts and allegations presented.
The court cited precedents stating that the 'proper test' is to determine the offence 'primarily and essentially' disclosed by the allegations to decide if consent is required.

cases.principle: The proper test to determine if sanction is required is to examine the allegations in the complaint to ascertain the offence 'primarily and essentially' disclosed, rather than relying merely on the sections mentioned.
To determine if sanction is necessary, it is the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts that matters, not the sections of law referred to in the complaint.
The necessity of sanction depends on the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts alleged in the complaint, not on the sections cited.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The determination of whether prior consent is necessary for the initiation of proceedings depends not on the specific sections of law mentioned in a complaint, but on the offence that is prima facie, primarily, and essentially disclosed by the facts and allegations contained within it.
obiter: Observations made in a minority judgment of S. K. Das, J., in Pramatha Nath.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Magistrate's jurisdiction to take cognizance of a case is determined at the initial stage based on the offences alleged in the police charge-sheet. Since the charge-sheet did not allege criminal conspiracy, the Magistrate lawfully took cognizance without prior consent under Section 196A(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The subsequent decision at the committal stage to frame a charge of criminal conspiracy does not retroactively invalidate the initial, lawful act of taking cognizance.
legal_tests_applied: The proper test should be whether the allegations made in the petition of complaint disclosed primarily and essentially an offence or offences for which a consent in writing would be necessary to the initiation of the proceedings within the meaning of s. 196A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The question whether sanction is necessary or not depends not on the sections referred to in a complaint but the offence prima facie disclosed by the facts alleged in it.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the Magistrate's later decision to frame a charge of criminal conspiracy at the committal stage could retroactively invalidate the initial cognizance of the case.
The court found that at the time of taking cognizance, the Magistrate was only considering the offences alleged in the charge-sheet, which did not include criminal conspiracy.
Therefore, the court concluded that consent under s. 196A(2) Cr.P.C. was not a condition precedent for the Magistrate to take cognizance of the case as it was initially presented.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the critical moment for determining the need for consent is when the Magistrate takes cognizance, not at a later stage of the proceedings.
